newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian president's old foe ready to work with him.
newsitem.headline: Russian president's old foe ready to work with him.

text.p: Alexander Rutskoi, who led an armed uprising against Russian President Boris Yeltsin in 1993, said on Thursday his old foe had changed enough in the past three years to deserve his support.

Rutskoi, who won a landslide poll victory last weekend to become governor of the central Kursk region, said he would concentrate on improving the economic and social situation in his new domain rather than confront the Kremlin.
"There is no sensation about my victory," the former airforce colonel, who won more than 70 percent support after only 36 hours of campaigning, told NTV commercial television.
"Now I need to look for a compromise," he added. "I need to meet the president and Prime Minister (Viktor Chernomyrdin) and start working hard."

In 1991 Yeltsin chose Rutskoi, an Afghan war veteran but a novice in politics, as his vice-president. But their relations soured as nationalist Rutskoi failed to find common language with Yeltsin's reformist team.

In 1993 Rutskoi led an armed uprising against Yeltsin after the president, overriding the constitution, dissolved the conservative Soviet-era parliament and ringed its White House headquarters with security forces.
Troops loyal to Yeltsin put down the revolt with heavy loss of life, pounding the White House where Rutskoi took shelter. Rutskoi then spent six months in prison before being amnestied by parliament.
Asked to explain his conciliatory tone, Rutskoi said it was not he who had changed. "Rutskoi remains Rutskoi, I cannot change myself...my criticism was constructive," he said.
Rutskoi said that dramatic changes in Yeltsin's entourage since the 1993 events had signalled a principal change in the Kremlin leader's policies.
"Where are those who surrounded Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin)? So ultimately Rutskoi was right."
Yeltsin, who faced a tough challenge from a communist rival in an election this summer, has replaced some liberal allies with more pragmatic figures in both his administration and government.

"Boris Nikolayevich decided to get rid of those persons who harmed," he said. "Russia has a practically new government which makes different decisions aimed at restoring law and order," he said, referring to new efforts to crack down on tax dodgers.
"I am ready to vote with both my hands for this new constructive course."
Rutskoi said old hostilities would not prevent him from dealing easily with Yeltsin.
"I know Boris Nikolayevich very well," he said. "I think he will make steps to work with me. I am not going to restart a conflict with the national leadership."

Rutskoi joined the election race in Kursk -- a struggling region which traditionally votes for communists -- less than two days before the poll after winning a court case against the local electoral commission which had refused to register him.
A communist candidate then withdrew, ensuring victory for Rutskoi, who also heads the hardline Congress of Popular and Patriotic forces grouping.
The governor's seat automatically makes Rutskoi a member of the Federation Council upper chamber of parliament.
Earlier on Thursday Yeltsin sent a short telegram of congratulations to Rutskoi, along with other governors elected last weekend.
"I hope your actions in this important post will help stabilise the socio-economic situation in the region," Yeltsin said in the telegram.
